title: Matrix Diagonal Sum
description: Brute force to optimized: checking every cell for diagonal membership versus computing both diagonals' positions directly via index formulas.

blocks.text: Given a square matrix mat, return the sum of its two diagonals: the PRIMARY diagonal (top-left to bottom-right) and the SECONDARY diagonal (top-right to bottom-left). Any element that belongs to both diagonals (only possible when the matrix has odd size, at its exact center) should be counted only once.

blocks.caption: For every row, add its primary-diagonal cell and secondary-diagonal cell, skipping a double-count at the center

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","A square n x n integer matrix mat"],["Output","The sum of every element on the primary diagonal plus every element on the secondary diagonal, counting the shared center cell (if any) only once"],["Goal","Compute this sum by visiting only the diagonal cells directly, not the entire matrix"],["Constraints","n == mat.length == mat[i].length; 1 <= n <= 100; 1 <= mat[i][j] <= 100"]]}

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["The PRIMARY diagonal always has row index equal to column index","Directly index mat[i][i] for every row i"],["The SECONDARY diagonal always has row index plus column index equal to n-1","Directly index mat[i][n-1-i] for every row i, derived instantly from i and n"],["The two diagonals can share exactly one cell (only when n is odd, at the exact center)","Skip adding the secondary-diagonal cell again whenever it's the same cell as the primary-diagonal one for that row"]]}

blocks.text: Given a square matrix, sum every element lying on either its top-left-to-bottom-right diagonal or its top-right-to-bottom-left diagonal, without double-counting the single cell where both diagonals cross (which only happens for odd-sized matrices).

blocks.title: Analogy: Summing Two Crossing Ribbons Laid Over a Grid
blocks.text: Like laying two ribbons diagonally across a square grid of numbered tiles, one running corner to corner in each direction, and wanting the total value of every tile touched by either ribbon. Where the two ribbons cross (only possible at the very center of an odd-sized grid), that single tile should only be counted once, even though both ribbons pass over it.

blocks.caption: Each row directly yields its own primary and secondary diagonal cell via simple index formulas

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["Primary diagonal: mat[0][0]=1, mat[1][1]=5, mat[2][2]=9, summing to 15","Primary sum: 15","These are the cells where row index equals column index"],["Secondary diagonal: mat[0][2]=3, mat[1][1]=5, mat[2][0]=7, summing to 15","Secondary sum: 15","These are the cells where row index plus column index equals n-1=2"],["The center cell mat[1][1]=5 is shared by both diagonals, so it's only counted once","Combined sum: 15 + 15 - 5 = 25","Subtracting one occurrence of the shared cell avoids double-counting it"],["Answer","25","This is the correctly combined diagonal sum"]]}

Secondary diagonal: 4 cells, each valued 1, summing to 4","Combined sum: 4 + 4 = 8","Since n is even, no cell is shared between the two diagonals at all"],["Answer","8","No double-counting adjustment is needed here, since the diagonals never overlap for an even-sized matrix"]]}

blocks.text: Before scanning every cell in the matrix to check whether it belongs to either diagonal, notice that both diagonals' cell positions are given directly by simple formulas based on the row index alone.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: The primary diagonal's cell in row i is always at column i, so mat[i][i] directly gives that cell, no searching needed.

Observation 2: The secondary diagonal's cell in row i is always at column (n - 1 - i), since the two column positions must always sum to n - 1 across the diagonal, again directly computable from i and n alone.

Observation 3: The two diagonals share a cell only when i equals (n - 1 - i) for some row, which happens only when n is odd, at the exact middle row.

Observation 4: Loop through each row once, adding mat[i][i] and mat[i][n-1-i], but skip adding the second one again whenever it's the same cell as the first (i.e., when n - 1 - i equals i).

Recognizing that both diagonal positions are directly computable, with no need to search or check every matrix cell, turns an apparently O(n squared) full-scan problem into a simple O(n) single loop.
This is a direct index-formula problem: every diagonal cell's position is computed directly from its row index, with a single conditional check to avoid double-counting the shared center cell.
Check every single cell in the matrix, testing whether it lies on either diagonal.

items: For every cell (i, j) in the matrix, check whether i equals j (on the primary diagonal) or i + j equals n - 1 (on the secondary diagonal).
If either condition holds, add that cell's value to the running total.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Every cell in the entire n x n matrix is visited, since this brute force does not yet exploit the direct-formula positions of diagonal cells.
The condition (i == j || i + j == n - 1) correctly identifies membership in either diagonal for any cell.
Since each qualifying cell is only visited once during the full scan, no separate double-counting adjustment is needed here.

blocks.text: Every cell is checked directly against both diagonal conditions, so the correct total is always found.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), visiting every cell in the matrix even though only about 2n of them ever qualify.
Space: O(1) extra.

Limitation: visiting every cell in the matrix ignores that the exact positions of every diagonal cell are already known directly from simple index formulas, without needing to check any non-diagonal cell at all.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force checks every cell in the matrix. Instead, loop through only the row indices (0 to n-1), directly computing each row's primary-diagonal cell (mat[i][i]) and secondary-diagonal cell (mat[i][n-1-i]) via simple formulas. Add both to the running total, except skip adding the secondary cell again when it coincides with the primary cell (which only happens at the middle row of an odd-sized matrix).
For each row i from 0 to n-1, add mat[i][i] to the total. Compute j = n - 1 - i; if j is not equal to i, also add mat[i][j] to the total.
Loop through row indices only, directly computing and summing both diagonal cells per row.

blocks.title: Final answer
blocks.text: The running total after all rows is 25, matching the expected answer.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), visiting only the n rows, each contributing at most 2 direct diagonal-cell lookups.
Space: O(1) extra.

Every primary-diagonal cell in row i is, by definition, at column i, and every secondary-diagonal cell in row i is at column (n - 1 - i), since the two diagonal endpoints (row 0 at column n-1, row n-1 at column 0) fix this relationship for every row in between. The only way these two formulas can point to the SAME cell is when i equals (n - 1 - i), which only has a solution when n is odd (at the exact middle row), so checking for that specific coincidence is sufficient to avoid double-counting.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What happens"],"rows":[["j (secondary column) is not equal to i","Both mat[i][i] and mat[i][j] are added to the total, as two distinct cells"],["j (secondary column) equals i (only possible mid-row of an odd-sized matrix)","Only mat[i][i] is added, since it's the same cell as the would-be secondary-diagonal cell"]]}

items: The loop iterates over row indices only (0 to n-1), never touching a full n-by-n grid of cell pairs.
j = n - 1 - i is computed directly from i and n, requiring no search or condition to locate the secondary-diagonal cell.
The if (j != i) check is the sole safeguard against double-counting, applying correctly regardless of whether n is even or odd.

blocks.text: When the exact positions of the cells of interest are given by simple, direct formulas (rather than needing to be searched for), visiting only those positions directly is far more efficient than scanning the entire structure.

items: Forgetting the double-counting adjustment entirely, which overcounts the shared center cell by exactly its value for any odd-sized matrix.
Using an incorrect formula for the secondary diagonal's column (e.g., n - i instead of n - 1 - i), causing an off-by-one indexing error.
Scanning the entire matrix (O(n squared)) when only the n diagonal cells per diagonal are ever actually needed.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Sum elements on specific diagonals of a matrix" points toward computing each diagonal's cell positions directly via simple index formulas (row==column for the primary, row+column==n-1 for the secondary), rather than scanning the whole matrix.

items: How would you generalize this to sum an arbitrary "offset" diagonal (not just the two main ones)? An offset diagonal parallel to the primary diagonal has a constant (row - column) value; iterating rows and computing the matching column via that offset generalizes the same direct-formula technique.

What if the matrix were not square (rows != columns)? The two main diagonals as defined here (corner to corner) only make clean sense for a square matrix; a non-square matrix would need a different, more careful definition of what "diagonal" means.

How would you sum diagonals in a 3D array (a cube)? This generalizes conceptually (using consistent index relationships across all three axes), though the specific formulas and the number of distinct "diagonals" become considerably more complex.

A direct index-formula technique for identifying diagonal cells, a building block reused conceptually in more complex diagonal-traversal problems (e.g., diagonal matrix traversal, anti-diagonal grouping) elsewhere in matrix problems.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n squared) time, O(1) space.
Optimized (direct diagonal index formulas): O(n) time, O(1) space.

items: Pattern: Direct index-formula computation of diagonal cell positions, avoiding a full matrix scan
Core Idea: Primary diagonal cells are at (i, i); secondary diagonal cells are at (i, n-1-i); skip double-counting when these coincide (odd n, middle row)
Time: O(n)
Space: O(1)
Most Important Observation: Both diagonals' cell positions are directly computable from the row index and matrix size, with no need to scan the full matrix
Interview Difficulty: Easy
One-line memory trick: Sum mat[i][i] and mat[i][n-1-i] for every row, skipping the second when it equals the first
